econyl.types: ECONYL is a regenerated nylon 6 sold in several product forms. The main textile line is nylon textile filament (NTF) yarn, supplied in fine deniers for hosiery, swimwear, activewear and lingerie, with flat and textured variants. A second major line is bulked continuous filament (BCF) yarn for carpets, which Aquafil also makes in its own carpet-yarn business. Aquafil publishes separate Environmental Product Declarations for its textile filament yarns, so specifications and impact figures should be matched to the exact product and EPD version.
econyl.fabrics: Textile ECONYL yarns go into swimwear and bikinis (usually warp-knit with elastane), leggings and sports bras, hosiery, lingerie, lightweight windbreakers, backpacks and bags, and tricot linings. Carpet yarns are tufted into commercial carpet tiles and broadloom. In most apparel, ECONYL nylon is combined with a substantial share of elastane or with other fibers, which affects the recycled share and end-of-life recyclability of the product.
econyl.quality: The content label must say nylon or polyamide; ECONYL appears only alongside it. Ask the brand for the ECONYL share of total fiber content, since swimwear often contains a significant elastane fraction. Aquafil's EPDs and any recycled-content certificate should name the yarn. Physically, good nylon swim fabric feels dense and springy, recovers quickly after stretching and is opaque when stretched; thin fabric that goes see-through or bags out is a construction issue, not a fiber issue. Be skeptical of claims that a product is 'made from fishing nets' without a stated share, as Aquafil uses several waste streams.
pros: Depolymerization to purified caprolactam gives nylon that Aquafil says matches virgin nylon 6 in quality, unlike many mechanically recycled plastics.
It uses post-consumer and post-industrial nylon waste, including carpet fluff and fishing nets, as feedstock.
Aquafil publishes third-party verified EPDs, giving auditable impact data.
The same route can in principle regenerate ECONYL products again at end of life if they are collected and are nylon 6.
cons: It is still a synthetic that sheds microplastic fibers in washing, like virgin nylon.
Most apparel uses blend it with elastane, which makes the finished garment hard to recycle.
Marketing emphasis on ocean fishing nets can overstate that feedstock's share.
Only nylon 6 can be regenerated this way; nylon 6,6 and mixed waste are excluded.
econyl.impact: Aquafil states that ECONYL nylon can reduce the global warming impact of nylon by up to 90% compared with nylon from oil, and that for every 10,000 tonnes of ECONYL raw material about 65,100 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions are avoided; it attributes part of this to renewable electricity at its plant. These figures come from Aquafil and its EPDs, which are third-party verified within the EPD system but use Aquafil's functional units and baselines. Chemical depolymerization itself needs heat and steam, so gains depend on the energy mix. At the use stage, nylon sheds microfibers in laundering like other synthetics; a 2021 review in Heliyon (Gaylarde and colleagues) summarizes evidence that laundering synthetic textiles is a major source of microfibers. Recycled origin does not change that persistence.
econyl.care: Swimwear and activewear in ECONYL nylon should be rinsed in cool fresh water soon after use to remove chlorine, salt and sunscreen, then hand washed or machine washed cold on a gentle cycle with mild detergent. Avoid fabric softener, which clogs knit structures and holds odor. Do not wring; press out water and dry flat in the shade, since UV degrades both nylon and elastane. Never tumble dry hot or iron swimwear; nylon softens on heating and elastane loses recovery. For other nylon garments, iron only on a low to medium setting. A wash bag reduces snagging and fiber shedding.
faq: Is ECONYL made from ocean plastic?

Partly, sometimes. Aquafil uses several nylon waste streams, including discarded fishing nets, carpet face fiber and industrial scrap. The share of fishing nets varies, so a product claim should state the specific content rather than implying all the nylon came from the sea.
Is ECONYL as strong as regular nylon?

Aquafil says yes, because the waste is broken down to caprolactam, purified and repolymerized into nylon 6, the same polymer as virgin nylon 6. Durability of a garment still depends on yarn denier, knit construction and elastane content.

Yes. Regenerated nylon is chemically nylon 6 and sheds fibers in washing like virgin nylon. Washing cold, using full but not overloaded machines, wash bags or filters, and washing less often reduce release.
notable: Aquafil states that every 10,000 tonnes of ECONYL raw material avoids about 65,100 tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions compared with oil-based caprolactam.
Nylon 6 suits this closed loop because it depolymerizes cleanly back to a single monomer, caprolactam, which can be distilled to high purity.
